outline.keyPoint: Your child comes home with homework in German grammar: underline the «Prädikat», name the «Dativobjekt». You may not read German, and that is fine. The good news is that the method behind it is simple and visual. Two tests, a handful of names. This video gives you the method and the words in about twelve minutes: what the Bavarian curriculum expects in Year six, «Jahrgangsstufe sechs», pupils aged about eleven to twelve, how the two tests work, the typical mistakes, and how to help at home.

The Bavarian curriculum is called the «LehrplanPLUS». In German for Year six, the topic belongs to «Sprachliche Strukturen untersuchen», examining the structures of the language. It lists the sentence parts, «Satzglieder», predicative, objects and adverbials, together with attributes and relative clauses, adverbial, subject and object clauses, word classes with their Latin names, active and passive, tenses, and compound and complex sentences. This video covers the sentence parts and the attribute; the «Prädikativ» and the clauses follow in other videos. Sentence parts are one central part of the topic, and the later work on clauses and commas builds on them.

Four things the curriculum points to, and that teachers typically practise with two tests. First: split a sentence into its parts with the rearranging test, the «Umstellprobe». Second: name the subject, the predicate and the objects with the question test, the «Frageprobe». Third: tell adverbials apart by meaning: time, place, manner, reason. Fourth: recognise an attribute, «Attribut», as part of a sentence part rather than a part of its own. Which of these appear in tests is decided by the teacher. Latin, if your child learns it, uses similar ideas of subject and object, so the work often pays off there too.

Sentence parts are found and named with two tests, not with definitions. The rearranging test shows where a sentence part begins and ends. The question test gives it a name. One observation holds everything together: in a German statement the predicate, the verb, always stands in second position. Let us walk through the three steps with a sentence like the ones in your child's exercise book. The captions on screen are in German, exactly as the child sees them in class.

The sentence: «Am Morgen füttert Lena die Katze im Garten». In the morning, Lena feeds the cat in the garden. The rearranging test, «Umstellprobe», moves the parts around without changing the meaning: «Lena füttert am Morgen die Katze im Garten». Whatever moves together is one sentence part, one «Satzglied». In the morning stays together, the cat stays together, in the garden stays together. The blocks in the picture are exactly these units. Five blocks, five sentence parts.

The question test, «Frageprobe», gives every block a name. Who feeds? «Wer?», or for things «Wer oder was?». Lena: the subject, «Subjekt». What does Lena do? «Was tut sie?» She feeds: the predicate, «Prädikat». Whom or what does she feed? «Wen oder was?» The cat: the accusative object. When? «Wann?» In the morning. Where? «Wo?» In the garden: two adverbials. The German questions appear above the blocks. Many teachers want pupils to know them by heart; your child's teacher will say how much. In Latin, similar questions return.

Here is the observation that holds everything together, and it is the biggest difference from English. In a German statement, an «Aussagesatz», the predicate stands in second position, whatever comes first. «Lena füttert am Morgen die Katze im Garten». «Am Morgen füttert Lena die Katze im Garten». The verb stays in slot two. Second position means the second sentence part, not the second word: in «Der kleine Hund bellt laut» the verb is the fourth word but the second block. English keeps the subject before the verb; German keeps the verb in second place and lets almost anything go first. Knowing this, your child finds the predicate much more easily.

Finally the names under the blocks: «Adverbiale», «Prädikat», «Subjekt», «Objekt», «Adverbiale». These are the terms your child writes in exercises. Most of them look like English words: subject, predicate, object, adverbial, attribute. The new ones to learn are «Satzglied», «Umstellprobe», «Frageprobe», «Akkusativobjekt», «Dativobjekt» and «Aussagesatz». Primary school may have used German words such as «Satzgegenstand» for the subject; which terms your child's teacher wants is written in the exercise book. More important than the word is the test behind it.

Subject and predicate are found quickly. Much of the work in this video lies in three groups: the objects, which differ by grammatical case, the adverbials, which differ by meaning, and the attributes, which are not sentence parts of their own at all. Each group has its question, and with that question every exercise can be solved. Here they are, with one example sentence each, read by the German voice.

«Gestern schenkte mir Oma ein Buch». Yesterday Grandma gave me a book. Two objects hide in this sentence. Whom or what did she give? «Wen oder was?» A book: the accusative object, «Akkusativobjekt». To whom? «Wem?» To me: the dative object, «Dativobjekt». The question points to the case, and the case gives the name. English shows case only in a few pronouns, such as me and him, and not on nouns or articles, so expect this to take your child a while. Two rarer objects exist, the «Genitivobjekt» and the «Präpositionalobjekt».

«Wir fahren morgen mit dem Zug nach München». We are going to Munich by train tomorrow. Three adverbials in one sentence. When? «Wann?» Tomorrow: an adverbial of time. By what means? «Womit?» By train: manner. Where to? «Wohin?» To Munich: place. The fourth kind asks for the reason, «Warum?», why. Your child also learns the labels «temporal», «lokal», «modal» and «kausal», and they appear in exercises. The English words are almost identical, which helps.

«Der kleine Hund bellt laut». The little dog barks loudly. The word «kleine», little, describes the dog more closely and is an attribute, «Attribut». The key point: an attribute is not a sentence part of its own but a part of one. The rearranging test proves it: «Laut bellt der kleine Hund». The attribute moves with its noun; it cannot be moved on its own. The question is «Was für ein?», what kind of. Attributes can be adjectives, genitives, a «Genitivattribut» such as «das Haus meiner Oma», or whole relative clauses, «Relativsatz».

A quick check for you. Your child looks at a sentence and says: «Ich muss das Prädikat unterstreichen». What are they looking for, and where in a German statement will they find it? Take a moment. You have seen the answer in the pictures of this chapter.

The «Prädikat» is the predicate, the verb part of the sentence, and in a German statement it stands in second position. So your child looks at the second slot: «Am Morgen füttert Lena», «Lena füttert am Morgen», the verb is always there. One thing to watch: the predicate can have two parts. In «Lena hat am Morgen die Katze gefüttert», has fed, the predicate is «hat» and «gefüttert» together, and the second part sits at the very end. Both parts must be underlined.

Five mistakes are common in many classes. All five are exposed by one of the two tests, so it pays to ask the right question rather than give the answer. You can do that in English; your child applies the test in German. Here are the five, two at a time, each with the question that helps.

Mistake one: mixing up word classes and sentence parts. A noun is a word class; a subject is a sentence part. «Katze» is a noun, and «die Katze» is, in our sentence, the accusative object, not the subject. Ask: who is doing something? Mistake two: counting an attribute as a part of its own, so «der kleine Hund» becomes two parts. Ask: can you put «kleine» alone at the start of the sentence? It cannot be done, so it belongs to the subject.

Mistake three: the predicate is taken too short. In «Lena hat am Morgen die Katze gefüttert» the predicate has two parts, «hat» and «gefüttert», forming a bracket around the sentence, the «Satzklammer». Ask: which verb words together say what happens? Look for «hat» in second place and «gefüttert» at the end; both are underlined. Mistake four: dative and accusative swapped, often because the articles sound alike. «Der Lehrer gibt den Kindern ein Rätsel». Ask the two questions: to whom does he give it? «Den Kindern». Whom or what does he give? «Ein Rätsel».

Mistake five is subtle. In the rearranging test the parts may only swap places; the meaning must stay the same. «Die Katze füttert Lena» is a grammatical sentence, but now the cat is feeding Lena, which was not meant. In a rearrangement every part keeps its role; here the cat has become the one who acts. Ask: does the sentence still say the same thing? If not, it was not a rearrangement but a new sentence. You can judge this from a translation, without any German.

You can help without speaking German, because the tests are mechanical and your child does the German part. Ten minutes a few times a week is a reasonable start. Here is a routine you can try, then a look at how this is tested and which topics come next.

Step one: your child picks a sentence from the exercise book or a school text, reads it aloud and translates it for you. That alone is useful practice. Then the rearranging test: they move the parts around two or three times and circle what travels together. Then the question test, in German: «Wer?», «Was tut er?», «Wen oder was?», «Wem?», «Wann?», «Wo?». You follow along with the translation. Three minutes, and close to what the school asks for.

Step two: ask for the reason, not the answer, and let your child explain in English or in your language. Why is «mir» a dative object? Because it answers «Wem?», to whom. Why is «kleine» not a sentence part of its own? Because it cannot move on its own in the rearranging test. A child who can explain a test has very likely understood it. If your child recites a rule but cannot justify it, that is the signal to go back to the picture with the blocks.

How is this tested? In the subject German, the big written tests, «Schulaufgaben», are mostly essays. In many classes grammar is checked in shorter tests, «Stegreifaufgaben», or as one part of a larger test, but this varies by school and teacher. Typical tasks: mark and name the sentence parts in a short text, tell the objects apart by case, classify adverbials by meaning, recognise attributes, and show the rearranging test in writing. What exactly your child's teacher asks is their decision; the exercise book is the best guide.

What comes next? In the same topic, compound and complex sentences follow: the «Satzreihe», two or more main clauses, and the «Satzgefüge», a main clause with a subordinate clause, «Nebensatz». With them comes the comma, «Komma», which German places by rule, not by feel: usually between main clauses, though often not before «und» or «oder», and always between main and subordinate clause. A subordinate clause like «weil es regnet», because it is raining, can itself be a sentence part, here an adverbial of reason. Knowing sentence parts helps a child recognise such clauses and place the comma correctly. Latin, if your child takes it, asks similar questions, so this work pays off twice.

In short: you do not need German to help with sentence parts. Two tests do the work. Whatever moves together in the «Umstellprobe» is a «Satzglied». Whatever answers a question in the «Frageprobe» has its name: «Subjekt», «Prädikat», «Objekt», «Adverbiale». Let your child apply the tests and explain them in any language, and ask the right question when something goes wrong. scenes.narration: The Bavarian curriculum is called the «LehrplanPLUS». In German for Year six, the topic belongs to «Sprachliche Strukturen untersuchen», examining the structures of the language. It lists the sentence parts, «Satzglieder», predicative, objects and adverbials, together with attributes and relative clauses, adverbial, subject and object clauses, word classes with their Latin names, active and passive, tenses, and compound and complex sentences. This video covers the sentence parts and the attribute; the «Prädikativ» and the clauses follow in other videos. Sentence parts are one central part of the topic, and the later work on clauses and commas builds on them.
scenes.onScreenTitle: The curriculum: D6 4.2 Sprachliche Strukturen untersuchen

scenes.narration: Four things the curriculum points to, and that teachers typically practise with two tests. First: split a sentence into its parts with the rearranging test, the «Umstellprobe». Second: name the subject, the predicate and the objects with the question test, the «Frageprobe». Third: tell adverbials apart by meaning: time, place, manner, reason. Fourth: recognise an attribute, «Attribut», as part of a sentence part rather than a part of its own. Which of these appear in tests is decided by the teacher. Latin, if your child learns it, uses similar ideas of subject and object, so the work often pays off there too.

Sentence parts are found and named with two tests, not with definitions. The rearranging test shows where a sentence part begins and ends. The question test gives it a name. One observation holds everything together: in a German statement the predicate, the verb, always stands in second position. Let us walk through the three steps with a sentence like the ones in your child's exercise book. The captions on screen are in German, exactly as the child sees them in class.

The sentence: «Am Morgen füttert Lena die Katze im Garten». In the morning, Lena feeds the cat in the garden. The rearranging test, «Umstellprobe», moves the parts around without changing the meaning: «Lena füttert am Morgen die Katze im Garten». Whatever moves together is one sentence part, one «Satzglied». In the morning stays together, the cat stays together, in the garden stays together. The blocks in the picture are exactly these units. Five blocks, five sentence parts.

The question test, «Frageprobe», gives every block a name. Who feeds? «Wer?», or for things «Wer oder was?». Lena: the subject, «Subjekt». What does Lena do? «Was tut sie?» She feeds: the predicate, «Prädikat». Whom or what does she feed? «Wen oder was?» The cat: the accusative object. When? «Wann?» In the morning. Where? «Wo?» In the garden: two adverbials. The German questions appear above the blocks. Many teachers want pupils to know them by heart; your child's teacher will say how much. In Latin, similar questions return.

Here is the observation that holds everything together, and it is the biggest difference from English. In a German statement, an «Aussagesatz», the predicate stands in second position, whatever comes first. «Lena füttert am Morgen die Katze im Garten». «Am Morgen füttert Lena die Katze im Garten». The verb stays in slot two. Second position means the second sentence part, not the second word: in «Der kleine Hund bellt laut» the verb is the fourth word but the second block. English keeps the subject before the verb; German keeps the verb in second place and lets almost anything go first. Knowing this, your child finds the predicate much more easily.
scenes.onScreenTitle: Step 3: the predicate in second position

scenes.narration: Finally the names under the blocks: «Adverbiale», «Prädikat», «Subjekt», «Objekt», «Adverbiale». These are the terms your child writes in exercises. Most of them look like English words: subject, predicate, object, adverbial, attribute. The new ones to learn are «Satzglied», «Umstellprobe», «Frageprobe», «Akkusativobjekt», «Dativobjekt» and «Aussagesatz». Primary school may have used German words such as «Satzgegenstand» for the subject; which terms your child's teacher wants is written in the exercise book. More important than the word is the test behind it.
scenes.onScreenTitle: The names of the sentence parts

scenes.narration: Subject and predicate are found quickly. Much of the work in this video lies in three groups: the objects, which differ by grammatical case, the adverbials, which differ by meaning, and the attributes, which are not sentence parts of their own at all. Each group has its question, and with that question every exercise can be solved. Here they are, with one example sentence each, read by the German voice.
scenes.onScreenTitle: The parts and their German names

scenes.narration: «Gestern schenkte mir Oma ein Buch». Yesterday Grandma gave me a book. Two objects hide in this sentence. Whom or what did she give? «Wen oder was?» A book: the accusative object, «Akkusativobjekt». To whom? «Wem?» To me: the dative object, «Dativobjekt». The question points to the case, and the case gives the name. English shows case only in a few pronouns, such as me and him, and not on nouns or articles, so expect this to take your child a while. Two rarer objects exist, the «Genitivobjekt» and the «Präpositionalobjekt».

«Wir fahren morgen mit dem Zug nach München». We are going to Munich by train tomorrow. Three adverbials in one sentence. When? «Wann?» Tomorrow: an adverbial of time. By what means? «Womit?» By train: manner. Where to? «Wohin?» To Munich: place. The fourth kind asks for the reason, «Warum?», why. Your child also learns the labels «temporal», «lokal», «modal» and «kausal», and they appear in exercises. The English words are almost identical, which helps.

«Der kleine Hund bellt laut». The little dog barks loudly. The word «kleine», little, describes the dog more closely and is an attribute, «Attribut». The key point: an attribute is not a sentence part of its own but a part of one. The rearranging test proves it: «Laut bellt der kleine Hund». The attribute moves with its noun; it cannot be moved on its own. The question is «Was für ein?», what kind of. Attributes can be adjectives, genitives, a «Genitivattribut» such as «das Haus meiner Oma», or whole relative clauses, «Relativsatz».

A quick check for you. Your child looks at a sentence and says: «Ich muss das Prädikat unterstreichen». What are they looking for, and where in a German statement will they find it? Take a moment. You have seen the answer in the pictures of this chapter.
scenes.onScreenTitle: The parts and their German names

scenes.narration: The «Prädikat» is the predicate, the verb part of the sentence, and in a German statement it stands in second position. So your child looks at the second slot: «Am Morgen füttert Lena», «Lena füttert am Morgen», the verb is always there. One thing to watch: the predicate can have two parts. In «Lena hat am Morgen die Katze gefüttert», has fed, the predicate is «hat» and «gefüttert» together, and the second part sits at the very end. Both parts must be underlined.

Five mistakes are common in many classes. All five are exposed by one of the two tests, so it pays to ask the right question rather than give the answer. You can do that in English; your child applies the test in German. Here are the five, two at a time, each with the question that helps.

Mistake one: mixing up word classes and sentence parts. A noun is a word class; a subject is a sentence part. «Katze» is a noun, and «die Katze» is, in our sentence, the accusative object, not the subject. Ask: who is doing something? Mistake two: counting an attribute as a part of its own, so «der kleine Hund» becomes two parts. Ask: can you put «kleine» alone at the start of the sentence? It cannot be done, so it belongs to the subject.

Mistake three: the predicate is taken too short. In «Lena hat am Morgen die Katze gefüttert» the predicate has two parts, «hat» and «gefüttert», forming a bracket around the sentence, the «Satzklammer». Ask: which verb words together say what happens? Look for «hat» in second place and «gefüttert» at the end; both are underlined. Mistake four: dative and accusative swapped, often because the articles sound alike. «Der Lehrer gibt den Kindern ein Rätsel». Ask the two questions: to whom does he give it? «Den Kindern». Whom or what does he give? «Ein Rätsel».

Mistake five is subtle. In the rearranging test the parts may only swap places; the meaning must stay the same. «Die Katze füttert Lena» is a grammatical sentence, but now the cat is feeding Lena, which was not meant. In a rearrangement every part keeps its role; here the cat has become the one who acts. Ask: does the sentence still say the same thing? If not, it was not a rearrangement but a new sentence. You can judge this from a translation, without any German.

You can help without speaking German, because the tests are mechanical and your child does the German part. Ten minutes a few times a week is a reasonable start. Here is a routine you can try, then a look at how this is tested and which topics come next.
scenes.onScreenTitle: Helping at home, and what comes next

scenes.narration: Step one: your child picks a sentence from the exercise book or a school text, reads it aloud and translates it for you. That alone is useful practice. Then the rearranging test: they move the parts around two or three times and circle what travels together. Then the question test, in German: «Wer?», «Was tut er?», «Wen oder was?», «Wem?», «Wann?», «Wo?». You follow along with the translation. Three minutes, and close to what the school asks for.
scenes.onScreenTitle: Step 1: one sentence from the exercise book

scenes.narration: Step two: ask for the reason, not the answer, and let your child explain in English or in your language. Why is «mir» a dative object? Because it answers «Wem?», to whom. Why is «kleine» not a sentence part of its own? Because it cannot move on its own in the rearranging test. A child who can explain a test has very likely understood it. If your child recites a rule but cannot justify it, that is the signal to go back to the picture with the blocks.
scenes.onScreenTitle: Step 2: let them explain, in any language

scenes.narration: How is this tested? In the subject German, the big written tests, «Schulaufgaben», are mostly essays. In many classes grammar is checked in shorter tests, «Stegreifaufgaben», or as one part of a larger test, but this varies by school and teacher. Typical tasks: mark and name the sentence parts in a short text, tell the objects apart by case, classify adverbials by meaning, recognise attributes, and show the rearranging test in writing. What exactly your child's teacher asks is their decision; the exercise book is the best guide.

What comes next? In the same topic, compound and complex sentences follow: the «Satzreihe», two or more main clauses, and the «Satzgefüge», a main clause with a subordinate clause, «Nebensatz». With them comes the comma, «Komma», which German places by rule, not by feel: usually between main clauses, though often not before «und» or «oder», and always between main and subordinate clause. A subordinate clause like «weil es regnet», because it is raining, can itself be a sentence part, here an adverbial of reason. Knowing sentence parts helps a child recognise such clauses and place the comma correctly. Latin, if your child takes it, asks similar questions, so this work pays off twice.
scenes.onScreenTitle: What comes next: clauses and commas

scenes.narration: In short: you do not need German to help with sentence parts. Two tests do the work. Whatever moves together in the «Umstellprobe» is a «Satzglied». Whatever answers a question in the «Frageprobe» has its name: «Subjekt», «Prädikat», «Objekt», «Adverbiale». Let your child apply the tests and explain them in any language, and ask the right question when something goes wrong. The German version of this guide and the lesson for children are on this channel. Subscribe for the next topic.

publish.description:
Your child has to underline the Prädikat and name the Dativobjekt, and you cannot read the sentence. This guide explains the two tests Bavarian schools use, the German grammar terms with their English meaning, and how to help at home without speaking German.

In this video:
• What the LehrplanPLUS expects in topic D6 4.2
• The rearranging test (Umstellprobe) and the question test (Frageprobe) in 3D pictures
• Subjekt, Prädikat, Akkusativobjekt, Dativobjekt, Adverbiale, Attribut: what they mean
• Why the German verb sits in second position, and how that differs from English
• Five typical mistakes and the question that corrects each
• A ten-minute routine at home, in any language

For whom: international parents of Year 6 pupils (Jahrgangsstufe 6) at a Gymnasium in Bavaria.
